Chapter 15Evaluation kitTeaching notes

How Search Decides What You See · Practical companion

Vendor questionnaire

Take the book’s questions into a demonstration, procurement discussion or renewal review. Record the vendor’s answer and supporting evidence, then record separately what your library could verify.

Use the nineteen core questions for every review. Add the specialist sections that match the product’s capabilities. Each question says what to listen for in the answer. Sub-questions are lettered, so an answer can cite Q13b; where an earlier answer covers a later prompt, cite its question ID and answer the remaining parts.

Question list only, for sending to a vendor in advance

  • Q01 What does the system infer, change and decide?
  • Q02 Who controls the retrieval trajectory?
  • Q03 Which retrieval and ranking components are used?
  • Q04 What role does the neural model perform?
  • Q05 What is the indexed unit?
  • Q06 How are passage results assembled?
  • Q07 How is the hybrid combined?
  • Q08 Is exact lexical matching retained?

  • Q11 What trained the relevance model?

  • Q14 Are model, index and ranking changes disclosed?
  • Q15 What does a search cost, and what limits apply?
  • Q16 What happens when a mode is retired?
  • Q17 How is performance evaluated, and on whose queries?
  • Q18 Are failure cases part of the evaluation?
  • Q19 Can the library compare behaviour across an update?

Ranking methods

  • E01 Before RRF

Generated answers (RAG)

  • G01 What is the retriever—lexical, dense, sparse, hybrid—and is the choice fixed, blended or routed per query?
  • G02 What is the indexed unit, and what unit reaches the model’s context (Chapter 8)?
  • G03 Is the query transformed before retrieval, and can the transformation be inspected (Chapter 11)?
  • G04 How many retrieved items reach the context, and how were they selected from the candidate set (Chapter 7 on top-k boundaries)?
  • G05 Does the model choose retrieval actions, or execute a fixed sequence (Chapter 12)?
  • G06 How is faithfulness evaluated—and, separately, how is retrieval evaluated (Chapter 14)?
  • G07 When the answer is wrong, can retrieval failure be distinguished from generation failure (Chapter 13)?
Include in this questionnaire

Core questions Q01–Q19 are always included.

On screen

Print on A4 at 100% scale with browser headers and footers off. The questionnaire provides writing space on paper. To type answers, copy the selected content into your document editor. Responses are not entered or saved on this page.

Before Q01: supported retrieval inputs

Before comparing query boxes, ask what the product accepts as a retrieval starting point. Only text, or also controlled fields, a seed record, citation links, saved judgements and API predicates? For an agentic mode, ask whether both the task brief and the queries generated from it can be exported.

Chapter 15: supported starting points

Supported inputs and export capabilities / evidence reference

Use each question’s source link for context. For a performance comparison, use the local retrieval evaluation kit. This questionnaire covers retrieval evaluation; it is not a complete institutional procurement or legal checklist.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Query interpretation, transformation and control

Q01 What does the system infer, change and decide?

  1. Does it recognise fields, filters or intent without changing the input; correct, map, expand or generate retrieval inputs; choose retrieval routes; or construct a later query from earlier results?
  2. Can users inspect and export the interpretation, every transformed input, each route and any feedback records?

Listen for what is recognised, what is rewritten or added, and whether each change can be seen and exported. “Our AI understands your question” describes none of them.

Q02 Who controls the retrieval trajectory?

  1. Is the sequence fixed in advance, chosen from branches the designer enumerated—whether a rule, a classifier or a model picks the branch—or planned by a model from what it has observed?
  2. If a model chooses, what tools, sources and iteration limits bound it?
  3. Can users see every query it ran, every source it consulted, every route it took and the point at which it decided to stop?

Listen for who picks the next step (a fixed sequence, a choice among named branches, or a model’s plan) and the limits on tools, sources and rounds. “Agentic” on its own does not answer this.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Retrieval coverage and architecture

Q03 Which retrieval and ranking components are used?

  1. Is there Boolean retrieval, BM25-like lexical ranking, dense retrieval or reranking?
  2. Do the components operate in parallel, sequentially or both, how many candidates survive each cut-off, and does the system select components by query or always combine them?

Listen for the components, the order they run in and the number of candidates kept at each cut-off. “Hybrid” or “semantic” without numbers is a label, not an answer.

Q04 What role does the neural model perform?

Naming a model does not describe an architecture. Is it parsing or rewriting the query, producing the first-stage query and passage vectors, expanding the vocabulary of a sparse index, jointly reranking candidates, or generating the final answer? These are different jobs with different failure modes, and a model can be present without doing the one you assumed.

Listen for a job for each named model: parsing, first-stage retrieval, sparse expansion, reranking or writing. “Powered by BERT” names a model, not a stage.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Retrieval coverage and architecture (continued)

Q05 What is the indexed unit?

Is the system retrieving titles, abstracts, passages, sections or complete articles? A product whose index holds only abstracts cannot match evidence that occurs only in the full text at that retrieval stage, however sophisticated its vectors are. Ask separately whether it later fetches the full text, and what it passes on as context.

Listen for the unit at each stage: what is indexed for retrieval and what is passed on later. “We search full text” should say at which stage.

Q06 How are passage results assembled?

If five chunks from the same paper match, are their scores combined, is only the best retained, or are five near-duplicate results shown?

Listen for one stated rule (combined, best passage only, or shown separately) and whether several passages from one paper can crowd out other papers.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Retrieval coverage and architecture (continued)

Q07 How is the hybrid combined?

A product may call itself hybrid because it contains two retrievers even when one signal rarely affects the final ranking. Ask where component lists are fused, whether a later stage reranks the merged candidates, what cut-offs apply, and whether users can inspect, compare or control the component result sets.

Listen for where the lists meet, the combining rule and the depth of each list. Two modes demonstrated side by side do not show how they are combined.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Exactness and failure testing

Q08 Is exact lexical matching retained?

Can users search identifiers, chemical strings, gene names, dataset titles and quoted phrases without semantic expansion quietly changing the task?

Listen for a way to switch expansion off, or a mode that matches the string exactly, demonstrated on your own identifiers rather than described.

Q09 How is text tokenised and analysed?

Ask how the lexical path treats case, punctuation, hyphens and identifiers, and whether query and document analysis are compatible. For a dense model, ask whether it uses word, subword, character or byte inputs and how unfamiliar or newly coined strings are tested.

Listen for concrete treatment of case, hyphens and identifiers on the lexical path, and a test of new or unusual strings on the dense path. “The model handles any vocabulary” is not a test.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Exactness and failure testing (continued)

Q10 How are exactness, negation and exclusions tested?

Ask for examples involving identifiers, contradictory claims, NOT-like intent and near-duplicate names — not only attractive paraphrase demonstrations.

Listen for failure cases the vendor has tested, including ones that went wrong. A demonstration made only of successful paraphrases does not answer this.

Q11 What trained the relevance model?

Web queries, question–answer pairs, citation links and scholarly relevance judgements teach different behaviours. How was the model adapted to the disciplines and document types being searched?

Listen for the kinds of training data and how the model was adapted to scholarly material. “Trained on millions of papers” says what it read, not what it was taught to rank.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Auditability and repeatability

Q12 Can users inspect why a result appeared?

  1. Can they move from the displayed record backwards through the retrieval route, transformed inputs, inferred constraints, any feedback records, matched evidence, ranking or reranking stages, and final fusion or display rules?
  2. Does the product distinguish a faithful execution trace from a helpful but post-hoc explanation?

Listen for whether the explanation records what actually ran or is written afterwards. A fluent “why this result” paragraph may be the second.

Q13 Can the search be documented and rerun?

  1. Can users export the original input; exact generated Boolean query, filters, expansions, subqueries or hypothetical text; retrieval route; ranking mode; model version; index date; k or threshold; and retrieved identifiers?
  2. When the same search is rerun, does the system reuse the saved transformation or ask an LLM to generate it again?

Listen for a list of what an export actually contains, and whether a rerun reuses the saved query or generates a new one.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Auditability and repeatability (continued)

Q14 Are model, index and ranking changes disclosed?

Does the vendor announce when an update may change results a user previously obtained, and is there any way to tell after the fact which version produced a saved search?

Listen for a change log or version identifier that can be tied to a saved search. “We continuously improve the model” means results can change without notice.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Cost, limits and continuity

Q15 What does a search cost, and what limits apply?

  1. Is pricing per seat, per query or per token?
  2. What are the rate and iteration limits, and what happens when one is reached — a refusal, a truncated result, or a silently shallower search?
  3. Does an agentic mode cost differently from the ordinary one, and can the library see per-query consumption?

Listen for prices and limits in numbers, and what the user sees when a limit is reached. A search that silently becomes shallower is the answer to watch for.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Institutional evaluation

Q17 How is performance evaluated, and on whose queries?

Average benchmark scores can hide failures on the query types that matter locally. A serious evaluation uses the institution’s own disciplines, vocabulary, languages, document types and known relevant records.

Listen for evaluation on queries like yours, with results broken down by query type. A single benchmark average or leaderboard rank does not answer this.

Q18 Are failure cases part of the evaluation?

A vendor’s demonstration shows what the system does well. The searches that matter for procurement are the ones a library already knows to be difficult.

Listen for willingness to run searches your library already knows are difficult. A vendor that offers only its own demonstration queries has not answered.

Vendor questionnaire · Chapter 15

Institutional evaluation (continued)

Q19 Can the library compare behaviour across an update?

If a saved set of local test queries can be rerun after a model, index or ranking change, a library can detect a regression that no release note mentions.

Listen for a way to rerun a saved query set after an update and compare the results. If the only record is a release note, regressions will go unseen.

Vendor questionnaire · Appendix E

Ranking methods

Include when discussing rank fusion, learning to rank or reranking. Mark individual methods not used by this product as Not applicable and record the reason.

E01 Before RRF

which retrievers supplied lists, how deep was each list, were they weighted equally, and how were duplicates handled?

Listen for the contributing lists, their depths and any weights. “We use RRF” on its own leaves every part of this open.

E02 Before LTR

which features and transformations were available, what supplied the labels, how were click and exposure biases handled, which objective and model were used, and when was it last retrained?

Listen for the features, where the labels came from and when the model was last retrained. Click labels without bias correction reward whatever was already shown first.

E03 Before reranking

which retriever produced the candidates, how many reached each later stage, what text and metadata did each stage see, and what was the latency budget?

Listen for candidate counts at each stage and what text each stage saw. A reranker cannot recover what the first stage did not return.
